summary: Case-insensitive substring search. Scans the haystack string a1 for the pattern a2, comparing each haystack byte against two case variants of the pattern byte produced by sub_589A35 and sub_58B465 (presumably a lowercase and uppercase normalization). Returns a pointer to the first matching run, or 0 when no match or either input is null. Consistent with callers such as DriverNameIDLookup, TrackNameDisplayIDLookup and StringMatchingWithCaseSensitiveCaseInsensitiveMo that match names and tokens.

operations.description: Early return 0 when the haystack a1 is null.
Early return 0 when the pattern a2 is null.
Call sub_589A35 with the current pattern byte to obtain the first case-normalized variant v6.
Call sub_58B465 with the current pattern byte to obtain the second case-normalized variant v7.
Loop body runs only while the haystack start byte *a1 is non-zero.
Scan the haystack from the current scan cursor until a terminating zero byte; the inner pattern run advances only on a match, otherwise the search resumes one byte past the last recorded run start.
Match test: current haystack byte *v5 equals either case variant v6 or v7 of the pattern byte.
Record the run start: when the run length v4 is zero, store the current scan cursor into v9 (match_start).
On a match, advance the pattern cursor, increment the run length, and if the pattern terminator is reached return v9 (match start).
On a mismatch, reset the run length to zero, rewind the pattern cursor to a2, move the scan cursor past the last recorded run start (v9 + 1, or v5 + 1 if none), and clear v9.
Return v9 (pointer to the first matching run) when the full pattern is found.
Return 0 when the haystack terminator is reached without a full match.

unresolved: Exact direction of the two case normalizations: sub_589A35 and sub_58B465 likely map a byte to lower and upper case, but which is which is unproven.
Behavior when the two case variants collide (e.g. a non-alphabetic byte) is unspecified by the evidence.
Byte vs. character semantics are identical here because the comparison is byte-wise on char-sized inputs.
